introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah describes a feast God prepares for all peoples on his mountain, where he will destroy death forever. In the Gospel, Jesus tells the parable of a king's wedding feast: those first invited refuse, so the king invites everyone from the streets. Paul says, I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Let us accept God's invitation, and come clothed for the feast.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord prepares a feast for us. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may go out to the highways and invite everyone to God's feast. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have refused God's invitation: that they may hear it again and come. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor and those who have no place at the world's tables: that they may be welcomed. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who mourn: that God may wipe away the tears from every face. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may be clothed in the grace of our Baptism and live worthy of God's invitation. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you invite all people to the wedding feast of your Son. Help us to accept your invitation with joy, and clothe us in the garment of your grace. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The wedding feast
reflection.body:
Isaiah paints a picture of heaven as a great banquet: "the LORD of Armies will make all peoples a feast of choice meat, a feast of choice wines." And at this feast God will do what no one else can: "He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." The people will say, "Behold, this is our God! We have waited for him."

In the Gospel, Jesus compares the Kingdom of Heaven to a king who gives a wedding feast for his son. He sends his servants to call the invited guests, but "they would not come." He sends more servants with a warmer invitation: "all things are ready. Come to the wedding feast!" But the guests make excuses, "one to his own farm, another to his merchandise," and some even mistreat the servants.

So the king says, "Go therefore to the intersections of the highways, and as many as you may find, invite to the wedding feast." The servants gather everyone they find, "both bad and good," and the hall is filled. God's invitation goes out to everyone.

But there is a final scene. The king finds a guest without a wedding garment, and he is thrown out. The invitation is free, but it asks for a response. The wedding garment has often been understood as the grace of Baptism and a life of conversion. We are welcomed as we are, but we are not meant to stay as we are.

Jesus ends: "For many are called, but few chosen." The invitation is for all; whether we accept it is up to us.

Paul, in prison, speaks of the strength that comes from Christ: "I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me."

This week, think about the excuses you make to God. Accept his invitation. And invite someone else to Mass or to prayer.
